name: Charlotte
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Charlotte: banking and fintech diligence, energy counterparties, NC Business Court support, asset research.
hero_lede: Charlotte is one of the largest banking centres in the United States, home to Bank of America and Truist and a growing energy and logistics base. TDSC scopes investigative consulting from Nashville for Charlotte matters, using public records and coordinating North Carolina-licensed investigators and counsel where local work is required.
intro: Charlotte is the largest city in North Carolina and the seat of Mecklenburg County, with an estimated population of about 965,000 in 2025, up from 874,579 at the 2020 census. It is widely described as the second-largest banking centre in the United States: Bank of America and Truist Financial are headquartered there, and Wells Fargo runs its East Coast regional headquarters in the city. Duke Energy and more than 240 energy companies anchor a sector the region markets as a new energy capital, Honeywell moved its corporate headquarters to Charlotte in 2018, and Atrium Health is the largest employer. NASCAR operations, trucking and logistics, and a busy airline hub round out the economy.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Charlotte because of what is concentrated there: large bank balance sheets, the vendors and fintech firms that serve them, energy infrastructure contractors, and fast-growing commercial real estate. A lender may need to understand a borrower's affiliates across the Carolinas; an acquirer may be buying a payments or software firm built to serve the banks; an energy client may be relying on a contractor whose principals have prior disputes. Litigators need background on parties and witnesses before proceedings in state or federal court. North Carolina's licensing rules for investigators and its specialised business court shape how that work is done.

matters.title: Bank vendor and fintech diligence
matters.text: Charlotte's large banks rely on technology, payments and outsourcing vendors, many of them local start-ups or acquisitions. We review ownership, principals' histories, litigation, regulatory actions and related companies so a bank, investor or acquirer understands who it is dealing with before contracting or closing.

matters.title: Energy contractor and supplier checks
matters.text: Utilities and energy firms in the region use contractors for construction, grid work and equipment. We examine corporate records, safety and regulatory history, litigation and connected entities across the Carolinas to identify undisclosed related parties, prior failures or integrity concerns affecting a contract award.

matters.title: Commercial lending and borrower affiliates
matters.text: Lenders financing Charlotte developers and operating companies often face borrowers organised through layers of limited liability companies. We map affiliates, guarantors' assets, liens, judgments and prior bankruptcies from public records to support credit decisions and workouts.

matters.title: Business court litigation support
matters.text: Complex corporate and commercial disputes in North Carolina may be designated to the North Carolina Business Court. We support counsel with corporate histories, witness and party backgrounds and document trail reconstruction, scoped to the court's procedures and the discovery available.

matters.title: Executive appointments in financial services
matters.text: Charlotte's headquarters base generates senior hires in banking, energy and industry. We compile court, regulatory, corporate, bankruptcy and media records across the states where a candidate has worked, applying consumer reporting consent rules where they apply and agreeing scope with counsel.

local_context.title: North Carolina investigator licensing
local_context.text: North Carolina regulates private investigators under the Private Protective Services Act, Chapter 74C of the General Statutes. The Private Protective Services Board, established within the Department of Public Safety, licenses individuals and agencies. The Act defines a private investigator broadly, covering contractual inquiries into a person's identity or conduct, the recovery of property, the causes of accidents and evidence for court proceedings, and requires a licence to engage in that work. TDSC coordinates North Carolina-licensed professionals for any fieldwork.

local_context.title: Courts serving Charlotte
local_context.text: State cases arising in Charlotte are heard in the Mecklenburg County Superior and District Courts. Complex business cases, including disputes over corporate law, securities and certain contracts, can be designated to the North Carolina Business Court, which has a judge sitting in Charlotte. Federal fraud, securities and commercial cases are heard in the US District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, which sits in the city.

local_context.title: Records and registries
local_context.text: North Carolina companies are registered with the Business Registration Division of the Secretary of State, which publishes registered agents, principal office addresses and annual reports naming officers or managers. Real property records for Charlotte are kept by the Mecklenburg County Register of Deeds, and court records are held by the Mecklenburg County Clerk of Superior Court. Research on regional businesses often extends to neighbouring counties and into South Carolina.

local_context.title: Financial services supervision
local_context.text: Although Charlotte hosts very large bank headquarters, primary supervision of national banks and bank holding companies is federal, through agencies such as the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve, while the North Carolina Commissioner of Banks supervises state-chartered institutions and certain non-bank lenders. Enforcement actions published by these regulators are a key source for diligence on Charlotte financial firms and their personnel.

tdsc_approach: TDSC has no office in Charlotte and works on Charlotte matters from Nashville. We agree the purpose with the client and its counsel first, whether a bank vendor review, an energy contract award, a credit decision, Business Court or federal litigation, or an executive appointment, and scope research to it. Sources include North Carolina Secretary of State filings, Mecklenburg County deed and court records, federal dockets, banking regulators' enforcement databases and records in South Carolina and other states where parties operate. Any fieldwork in North Carolina is carried out by professionals licensed under the Private Protective Services Act. Reports set out sources and confidence levels so counsel and compliance teams can rely on them.

faqs.q: Does an investigator need a North Carolina licence to work in Charlotte?
faqs.a: Yes. The Private Protective Services Act, Chapter 74C of the North Carolina General Statutes, requires anyone who conducts investigations for hire to be licensed by the Private Protective Services Board, which sits within the Department of Public Safety. TDSC does not hold a North Carolina licence and coordinates licensed local professionals for any work in the state.

faqs.q: Where are complex business disputes heard in Charlotte?
faqs.a: State cases start in Mecklenburg County courts, and qualifying complex business cases can be designated to the North Carolina Business Court, which has a judge in Charlotte. Federal matters go to the Western District of North Carolina. Counsel chooses the forum; we tailor research to its procedures and the discovery available.

faqs.q: Can you review a fintech vendor serving Charlotte banks?
faqs.a: Yes. We identify the vendor's owners, principals and affiliates through state entity records, then review litigation, regulatory actions, bankruptcies, media coverage and any connections to sanctioned or high-risk parties. The aim is to give the bank or investor a documented picture of who controls the vendor and what history is attached to it.

faqs.q: Which records matter for asset research in Charlotte?
faqs.a: The Mecklenburg County Register of Deeds holds property records and the Clerk of Superior Court holds civil judgments and filings. We combine these with Secretary of State entity records, UCC filings and records in neighbouring counties and South Carolina, since Charlotte-area owners frequently hold property and companies across the state line.

faqs.q: Do you research executives joining Charlotte banks?
faqs.a: Yes. We compile court, regulatory, corporate, bankruptcy and media records from the states where a candidate has lived and worked, including published enforcement actions by banking and securities regulators. Where consumer reports are involved, federal and state consent rules apply, and we agree the scope with counsel and human resources first.
